messages.author: 3b38808984465857
messages.subject: Extracting generated quantities using Rstan
parts: I am just going through some of the arm models I have written to tidy them up before they go on github. Since a lot of the code in arm is in R, I arranged my files in the same manner as with the original bugs files. That is, I also want to rewrite the bits of R code in the book (there are a few typos which I don't want to leave unaddressed) and use rstan to allow for relatively compact code. Hereby I was wondering if there is a quick way to access generated quantities in rstan (such as model predictions). I browsed through the little guide on RStan, but could not find a quick way of doing so. I might be missing out the obvious here, but it would make some of my code a lot shorter and a lot nicer to read.

On 7/17/13 4:59 PM, Alexej Proskynitopoulos wrote:
> I am just going through some of the arm models I have written to tidy them up before they go on github.

I would recommend committing early and often and pushing
to GitHub. It provides backup and there's not much downside
to a project where you're not going to break tests.

> Since a lot of
> the code in arm is in R, I arranged my files in the same manner as with the original bugs files.

You mean the original BUGS files with ARM's distribution?
I haven't looked at the original distro, so I don't know
what you mean here.

If you could coordinate with Peter so all the code's organized
the same way, that would be ideal.

> That is, I also want to
> rewrite the bits of R code in the book (there are a few typos which I don't want to leave unaddressed) and use rstan to
> allow for relatively compact code.

You mean the R code that calls the R2WinBUGS, or
R code that calls lmer, etc.?

I'd concentrate on the former. When we've recreated
the lmer functionality in R, we can code all that, too.

And some of it we can probably code with Ben's new
tools.

Do let Andrew know about typos, though.

> Hereby I was wondering if there is a quick way to access generated quantities in
> rstan (such as model predictions). I browsed through the little guide on RStan, but could not find a quick way of doing
> so. I might be missing out the obvious here, but it would make some of my code a lot shorter and a lot nicer to read.

You should be able to access variables declared in
the generated quantities block of a Stan model just
like the other parameters using extract.

It'd be great if these predictive quantities could be
coded in Stan instead of in R.

- Bob

@Peter: Good! I will go over it shortly. It is great to hear that we are using the same setup then!

Speaking of the 'Matt Trick', there is something that is bothering me. I have recently been optimizing some of the models I implemented so far and wanted to use it to make things more efficient. However, I am not sure if I am doing it correctly. I read the relevant chapters in the Stan Guide about reparametrization, but the models I end up with seem to be doing slightly worse in terms of speed and effective sample size. For example, consider the following simple varying intercept multilevel model:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;                                           
    int<lower=1> J;                                            
    int<lower=1,upper=J> j[N];                                 
    real x[N];                                                 
    real y[N];
}

parameters {
    real b;                                                    
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;
    real a[J];                                             
    real mu_a;                                                 
    real<lower=0> sigma_a;
}

model {
    b ~ normal(0,100);                                         
    mu_a ~ normal(0,100);                                                                                                                
    a ~ normal(mu_a,sigma_a);                              
   
    for (n in 1:N)                                            
        y[n] ~ normal(a[j[n]]+b*x[n],sigma_y);                          
}

What I did so far is

data {
...
}

parameters {
...
    vector[J] a_error;
}
   
transformed parameters {

    vector[J] alpha;
    alpha<-a_error*sigma_a+mu_a;
}

model {
...    
    a_error ~ normal(0,1);
}

I would greatly appreciate it, if someone could apply the Matt trick to this model and let me know their results (as well as the model they end up with). I realize that this is a very simple question/model (I tried the same trick with more complicated ones) but I do not like the results I currently end up with.

> y[n] ~ normal(a[j[n]]+b*x[n],sigma_y);
> }
>
> What I did so far is
>
> data {
> ...
> }
>
> parameters {
> ...
> vector[J] a_error;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>
> vector[J] alpha;
> alpha<-a_error*sigma_a+mu_a;
> }
>
> model {
> ...
> a_error ~ normal(0,1);
> }
>
> I would greatly appreciate it, if someone could apply the Matt trick to this model and let me know their results (as
> well as the model they end up with). I realize that this is a very simple question/model (I tried the same trick with
> more complicated ones) but I do not like the results I currently end up with.

Yes, that looks right to me, assuming that "alpha" in
the new model is used like "a" in the original. Do you get
the same results?

If you want someone else to run it, you should point them to
the data and full model somewhere under version control.

We don't want to use priors with sd=100, either. Andrew will have
some opinion about what to use.

You should also have a prior on sigma_a and sigma_y. Again,
Andrew should have some opinion about what to do for his book's models.

If you wouldn't mind, can you follow the style guide at the end
of the manual in laying out the models? That'd be 2 spaces of
indentation, not 4, and spaces around all operators and assignment.
Also, no tabs if that accounts for some of the uneven spacing in the e-mail.

- Bob

> In my particular example, convergence was pretty fast even with the crude model.
> But with the Matt trick it was even faster. R and Stan code are attached, and results are below.

Ten times faster, assuming the time was the same and
that the result holds up over multiple runs.

Nice illustration of why it's effective sample size/second that matters.

I think it's great that Michael put it in the command-line output for Stan 2;
we should roll it into print for R, too.
> P.S. I think it would be great if Matt and Mike (or some other combination of people) were to write a short paper explaining the Matt trick.

With a clean result like this on a very prototypical model,
the paper should be easy. I'd suggest:

Michael: frame the paper and explain the geometry
Alexeij and Peter: do the experiments, create graphs, fill out paper
Andrew: initial implementation and model

Matt could also do what I have Michael penciled in for, but
then it would be tacky to call it the "Matt trick".

- Bob
